before:
So set one boundary. "What's a 'boundary'?", I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that's costing you too much (money, time, whatever it is). Throw the moldy bread in the trash. Handle that task you've been putting off, or the tax man, or your DUIs in Maryland, even if all you do today is open the envelope. Keep one small promise to your little one. Clean your room! And if a relationship keeps making you less safe, leave it, which is not a small thing at all, I know. Your little one has had enough grown-ups who said sweet things and then did nothing, so this is how they start to believe you.

You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack. "What's an 'internal attack'?" Calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again, for one. Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them. If they're sarcastic about it, you let it go by instead of snapping back. They don't trust you yet, and you don't ask them to. They complain about something, they're right, and you say so. All of that shows as clearly to them as the clean room did. It's proof you love them, but they can still tell the difference between being put up with and being loved.
after: (Not written yet. The next paragraph will be about afterward: looking at what actually happened; if you didn't do it, not assuming you know why (fear, not being sure of the goal, not knowing how, exhaustion, something practical); doing it without feeling better right away isn't failure, and doing it doesn't prove it helped; keeping the acts that make things safer, closer, more capable or more enjoyable, not the ones that just earn a tick. Leave all of that to it.)
brief:
- Guide paragraph 3, folded in here: little or no warmth for your little one yet (Nurturer absent) -> the Protector's acts can still begin the relationship. First care: maybe a meal, maybe cancelling an obligation. Warmth later.
- First half of guide paragraph 4: one act from the paragraphs before, made specific. When? Smallest first step? Help or resources needed? A predictable hard moment -> a short rehearsal beforehand.
Note: the paragraph before ends on "they can still tell the difference between being put up with and being loved." Don't contradict the article's stance that love matters and doesn't have to wait for trust (the next section says so); this is about where you can start, not about love being unnecessary. "The Nurturer" and "the Protector" are already introduced in the article, as two of the three jobs one grown-up does (the third is the Guide).
Your first sentence will be read together with the last lines of the paragraph before. There, openers that start a new topic ("Then there's…", "Some of it happens…") or keep a run of commands going have failed.
What earlier drafts of this paragraph did (all read as AI): three opened by asking "what if there isn't much love there yet?" and then listed the acts. Three more wrote "you can start with the Protector anyway" and "that's the Nurturer not showing up yet", rehearsed "in the car" and needed "a ride". Advice worded as "you can…", "you could…", "it might help to…" piles up into a coaching voice.
Limits: don't invent facts about the author's life, and don't write "I" for him; never call the inner child "the kid"; don't reuse the paragraphs before's items (the boundary, moldy bread, tax man, clean room, keys, sarcasm). The locked door is already earlier in the article, and the phone at midnight belongs to another paragraph, so leave both out.
length: four to seven sentences, 80 to 120 words
